nameStory: The Atlantic Thread Herring gets its name from the incredibly long, thread-like extension on its dorsal fin that trails behind like a delicate streamer. This distinctive 'thread' can be longer than the fish's head and makes it unmistakable among New England's herring family. The name perfectly captures this fish's most eye-catching feature that seems to flutter through the water like a silver ribbon.
description: The Atlantic Thread Herring is a sleek, silvery fish that looks like it's wearing a flowing cape thanks to its signature long dorsal fin extension. With its dark blue-gray back fading to bright silver sides and a clean white belly, it has the classic herring body plan but with that unmistakable trailing thread. These fish typically grow to about 15 inches long, making them a medium-sized member of the herring family. They're primarily tropical fish that occasionally venture into New England's warmer waters.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: The dorsal fin has an extremely long, thread-like extension that trails behind the fish like a streamer - this is the defining feature you can't miss

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Typical herring profile with a compressed, streamlined body that feels firm and muscular when handled, with a relatively small head compared to the body

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark blue-gray back that transitions sharply to bright silvery sides with a clean white belly - the scales have a mirror-like quality that reflects light brilliantly

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Grows up to 15 inches in length, making it larger than most sardines but smaller than adult shad

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in shallow coastal waters, harbors, and bays where they form schools - prefer warmer water temperatures

habitat: In New England, Atlantic Thread Herring are most likely found in shallow coastal waters, protected harbors, and warm bays, especially during the warmer months. They prefer areas with good plankton concentrations and tend to stay in relatively shallow water where they can feed efficiently. These fish are at the very northern edge of their range in New England waters, so they're most common in the warmer southern portions of the region.

seasonality.spring: May begin appearing in New England waters as temperatures warm, typically in protected bays and harbors first.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to encounter them in New England, when warm water temperatures bring them north from their usual southern range.
seasonality.fall: Still present in warmer coastal areas, but beginning to move south as water temperatures start dropping.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in New England waters, as they retreat to warmer southern waters for the cold months.

funFact: Despite being called a herring, the Atlantic Thread Herring is actually more closely related to gizzard shads and has a muscular stomach that helps it grind up its food - just like a bird's gizzard!
confusionNotes: Often confused with scaled sardines by anglers, but the thread herring's long dorsal fin extension is unmistakable once you know to look for it. Remember: if it has the 'thread,' it's a thread herring - no other similar fish in our waters has this trailing fin feature.
contextualKnowledge: These fish are actually tropical species that only occasionally venture into New England waters during warm periods, which explains why there's only been one recorded observation in the region. They're much more common from the Mid-Atlantic south to Brazil.
compareHints: As the only thread herring species in our region, it's most similar to other members of the herring family like sardines and true herrings. However, the long thread-like dorsal fin extension immediately sets it apart from all other silvery schooling fish in New England waters. Unlike true herrings, thread herrings have that specialized gizzard-like stomach and tend to stay in shallower, warmer coastal areas.
